goals: Classify haloalkanes and haloarenes by structure and name them by the IUPAC system
Explain the methods of preparation and the physical properties of halogen compounds
Understand the mechanisms of [[sn2]] and [[sn1]] reactions and the order of reactivity
Understand chirality, enantiomers and racemic mixtures; recognise inversion and retention of configuration
Predict the major product of an elimination reaction with [[zaitsev]]; explain the low reactivity of aryl halides

haloalkane.def: A compound in which one or more hydrogen atoms of an alkane are replaced by halogen atoms (sp³ C–X bond).

haloarene.def: A compound in which a halogen atom is attached to an sp² carbon of an aromatic ring (aryl halide).

allylic.def: A halide in which the halogen is attached to an sp³ carbon next to a C=C double bond.

benzylic.def: A halide in which the halogen is attached to an sp³ carbon that is bonded to an aromatic ring.

vinylic.def: A halide in which the halogen is attached to an sp² carbon of a C=C double bond.

geminal.def: In a geminal dihalide both halogens are on the same carbon; in a vicinal dihalide they are on adjacent carbons.

nucleophile.def: An electron-rich species that can donate an electron pair and attacks a positive centre.

leaving.def: The group that leaves with the bonding electron pair in a substitution reaction (e.g. a halide ion). I⁻ is the best leaving group.

sn2.def: A one-step, second order reaction; the nucleophile attacks from the back side and the configuration is inverted.

sn1.def: A two-step, first order reaction; a carbocation forms first and is then attacked by the nucleophile; racemisation occurs.

ambident.def: A nucleophile with two nucleophilic centres (e.g. CN⁻, NO₂⁻) that can bond in two ways.

chiral.def: A molecule or object that cannot be superimposed on its mirror image; it has an asymmetric carbon and is optically active.

enantiomer.def: Two stereoisomers that are mirror images of each other and cannot be superimposed.

racemic.def: An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers; it is optically inactive (rotation zero).

inversion.def: Reversal of the arrangement of the groups around the central carbon during a reaction (SN2).

zaitsev.def: In dehydrohalogenation the major product is the alkene with more alkyl groups on the doubly bonded carbons.

grignard.def: RMgX obtained from an alkyl halide and Mg in dry ether; a very reactive organometallic compound.

freon.def: Chlorofluoro derivatives of methane and ethane (e.g. CCl₂F₂); used for cooling but harmful to the ozone layer.

blocks.text: Replacing one or more hydrogen atoms of an aliphatic or aromatic hydrocarbon by halogen gives a [[haloalkane]] or a [[haloarene]]. These compounds are used in industry and daily life — as solvents, in the synthesis of organic compounds, and in medicine (chloramphenicol, thyroxine, chloroquine, halothane).
**By the number of halogen atoms:** compounds with one, two or more halogen atoms are called mono-, di- and polyhalogen compounds (tri-, tetra-, ...). **By the hybridisation of the carbon:**

items: **With an sp³ C–X bond:** (a) alkyl halides (R–X) — primary (1°), secondary (2°) or tertiary (3°) according to the carbon carrying the halogen; (b) allylic halides — halogen on an sp³ carbon next to C=C; (c) benzylic halides — halogen on an sp³ carbon next to an aromatic ring.
**With an sp² C–X bond:** (a) vinylic halides — halogen on an sp² carbon of C=C; (b) aryl halides — halogen on an sp² carbon of an aromatic ring.

blocks.text: **Nomenclature:** In the common system the name of the alkyl group is followed by the name of the halide (n-propyl bromide, isopropyl chloride). In the IUPAC system they are named as haloalkanes (1-bromopropane, 2-chloropropane). In haloarenes the positions of two halogens are shown by o-, m-, p- or by the numbers 1,2 ; 1,3 ; 1,4.

When two halogens are on the same carbon it is a [[geminal]] dihalide (alkylidene halide, e.g. CH₃CHCl₂); when they are on adjacent carbons it is a vicinal dihalide (alkylene dihalide, e.g. ClCH₂CH₂Cl); in the IUPAC system both are dihaloalkanes (1,1-dichloroethane, 1,2-dichloroethane).

blocks.label: Example 1
blocks.text:
Some isomers of C₅H₁₁Br:
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂Br — 1-bromopentane (1°)
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(Br)CH₃ — 2-bromopentane (2°)
(CH₃)₂CBrCH₂CH₃ — 2-bromo-2-methylbutane (3°)
(CH₃)₃CCH₂Br — 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (1°)

sections.title: The C–X Bond and Physical Properties

blocks.text: Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polar: carbon is partly positive (δ⁺) and the halogen partly negative (δ⁻). Atoms become larger from F to I, so the C–X bond length increases from C–F to C–I and the bond enthalpy falls.

**Melting and boiling points:** Dipole–dipole attraction and van der Waals forces between haloalkane molecules are strong, so chlorides, bromides and iodides boil much higher than alkanes of similar mass. For the same alkyl group the order of boiling points is RI > RBr > RCl > RF (van der Waals forces grow with molecular size). Branching lowers the boiling point — n-butyl bromide 375 K, sec-butyl 364 K and tert-butyl 346 K.

blocks.name: halide-bp
blocks.title: Comparing boiling points of halides
blocks.caption: Change the alkyl group and the halogen to see the trend in boiling points. Then look at the effect of branching on the butyl bromides.

blocks.text: Go from CH₃X to C₃H₇X and compare Cl, Br and I each time. Which factor raises the boiling point more — the size of the group or the halogen?

The isomers of dichlorobenzene have similar boiling points, but the melting point of the para isomer is higher than that of the ortho and meta isomers (323 K, 256 K and 249 K), because the para isomer is more symmetrical and packs better in the crystal lattice.

**Density:** Density increases with the number of halogen atoms or the atomic mass of the halogen (n-C₃H₇Cl 0.89 g/mL, n-C₃H₇Br 1.335, n-C₃H₇I 1.747; CH₂Cl₂ 1.336, CHCl₃ 1.489, CCl₄ 1.595). **Solubility:** Haloalkanes are only slightly soluble in water, because the energy needed to break hydrogen bonds in water is more than the energy released by haloalkane–water attraction. But they dissolve easily in organic solvents.

**1. From alcohols:** The –OH group of an alcohol is replaced by a halogen to give an alkyl halide. Thionyl chloride (SOCl₂) is the most convenient reagent because the by-products SO₂ and HCl are gases, so a pure product is obtained. Primary and secondary alcohols react with HX in the presence of ZnCl₂; tertiary alcohols react with concentrated HCl at room temperature. The order of reactivity of alcohols is 3° > 2° > 1°. Aryl halides cannot be made this way, because the C–O bond in phenol has partial double bond character.

R–OH + HX →(ZnCl₂) R–X + H₂O
R–OH + SOCl₂ → R–Cl + SO₂ + HCl
3R–OH + PX₃ → 3R–X + H₃PO₃     R–OH + PCl₅ → R–Cl + POCl₃ + HCl
blocks.label: From alcohols

blocks.text: **2. From hydrocarbons:** (i) Free radical halogenation of alkanes (Cl₂/UV or heat) — rarely used because a complex mixture of products is formed. (ii) Addition of HX to alkenes — with propene, 2-halopropane is the major product by Markovnikov's rule. (iii) Addition of X₂ to alkenes (Br₂ in CCl₄) — a vicinal dibromide; the red colour disappears (a test for unsaturation). (iv) Electrophilic substitution of aromatic hydrocarbons (Fe or FeCl₃ catalyst) — a mixture of ortho and para isomers.

**3. Halogen exchange:** The reaction of an alkyl chloride or bromide with NaI in dry acetone is the **Finkelstein reaction** — NaCl or NaBr precipitates, so the reaction goes forward (Le Chatelier's principle). Heating an alkyl chloride/bromide with AgF, Hg₂F₂, CoF₂ or SbF₃ gives a fluoride — the **Swarts reaction**. **4. From amines (Sandmeyer's reaction):** A primary aromatic amine is converted to a diazonium salt with NaNO₂ + HX at 273–278 K; reaction with Cu₂X₂ gives an aryl chloride or bromide, and with KI an aryl iodide.

blocks.label: Example 2
blocks.text:
How many monochloro compounds form in the free radical monochlorination of (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₃?
There are four kinds of hydrogen: (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂Cl, (CH₃)₂CHCH(Cl)CH₃, (CH₃)₂C(Cl)CH₂CH₃ and CH₃CH(CH₂Cl)CH₂CH₃ — four isomers.

The C–X bond of an alkyl halide is polar, so the carbon attached to the halogen is partly positive. A [[nucleophile]] (Nu⁻) is electron-rich, so it attacks this carbon and the halogen leaves as a halide ion ([[leaving]]). Such a reaction is a nucleophilic substitution:
R–X + Nu⁻ → R–Nu + X⁻

The cyanide (CN⁻) and nitrite (NO₂⁻) ions have two nucleophilic centres; such nucleophiles are called [[ambident]]. KCN is ionic and bonds through carbon to give an alkyl cyanide (the C–C bond is more stable); AgCN is covalent, so the free electron pair on nitrogen bonds and gives an isocyanide.

**(a) The [[sn2]] reaction:** This takes place in one step. The nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite to the leaving group; the new bond forms while the old bond breaks. In the transition state the carbon has five bonds and the three C–H bonds lie in one plane. As a result the **configuration is inverted** — like an umbrella turned inside out by the wind. Rate = k [R–X][Nu⁻] — second order. Greater steric hindrance slows the reaction: the order of reactivity is CH₃X > primary > secondary > tertiary.

**(b) The [[sn1]] reaction:** This occurs in polar protic solvents (water, alcohol). In the first (slow, rate determining) step the C–X bond breaks and a planar sp² carbocation forms; in the second (fast) step the nucleophile attacks. Rate = k [R–X] — first order. The more stable the carbocation, the faster the reaction, so the order of reactivity is tertiary > secondary > primary > CH₃X. Allylic and benzylic halides give resonance-stabilised carbocations, so they are reactive in SN1. For the same alkyl group, R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F (in both kinds of reaction).

blocks.label: Example 3
blocks.text:
Which of (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br and CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br is more reactive in SN1?
(CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br — because the carbocation formed from it is more stable (it can rearrange to a tertiary one by a hydride shift); in SN2, however, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br is more reactive because it has less steric hindrance.

Ordinary light becomes plane polarised when it passes through a Nicol prism. When such light passes through a solution of some compounds its plane is rotated; such compounds are **optically active**. A compound that rotates the plane to the right is dextrorotatory (+ or d) and to the left laevorotatory (− or l). Two such optically active isomers are **optical isomers**.

The cause of optical activity is molecular asymmetry. If four different atoms or groups are attached to a carbon atom, that carbon is an **asymmetric carbon** (stereocentre). Such a molecule cannot be superimposed on its mirror image — just like the right and left hand. It is [[chiral]] and the property is chirality. Two isomers that are mirror images but cannot be superimposed are [[enantiomer]]s. Propan-2-ol is achiral (two groups are the same), but butan-2-ol, 2-chlorobutane and 2-bromopropanoic acid are chiral.

The physical properties (melting point, boiling point, solubility) of the two enantiomers are the same; only the direction of rotation of plane polarised light differs, with the same magnitude. If one is dextrorotatory the other is laevorotatory. An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers is optically inactive — a [[racemic]] (±) mixture. Converting an enantiomer into a racemic mixture is **racemisation**.

blocks.name: chiral
blocks.title: Chiral molecules and optical rotation
blocks.caption: Choose a molecule and see whether it has an asymmetric carbon. Then change the ratio of the (+) and (−) enantiomers and see the rotation of light.

blocks.text: Choose 2-bromobutane and set the (+) and (−) ratio to 50 : 50. What is the rotation and why? Then look at propan-2-ol.

**Stereochemical outcome:** In SN2 the **configuration is inverted** — optically active (+)-2-bromooctane gives (−)-octan-2-ol. In SN1 the nucleophile can attack the planar carbocation from either side with equal probability, so **racemisation** occurs and a (±) mixture forms. If the bond to the chiral centre is not broken in the reaction, the **configuration is retained** (e.g. (−)-2-methylbutan-1-ol with HCl gives (+)-1-chloro-2-methylbutane; the sign of rotation changes although the configuration is retained).

blocks.label: Example 4
blocks.text: Is 2-chlorobutane chiral or achiral? C-2 carries –H, –Cl, –CH₃ and –CH₂CH₃ — four different groups; so C-2 is asymmetric and the compound is chiral. 2-Chloropropane is achiral because C-2 carries two –CH₃ groups.

sections.title: Elimination, Reactions with Metals and Reactions of Haloarenes

blocks.text: **Elimination reaction:** When a haloalkane with a β-hydrogen is heated with an alcoholic solution of KOH, the halogen from the α-carbon and a hydrogen from the β-carbon are removed as HX and an alkene forms (β-elimination or dehydrohalogenation). If there are β-hydrogens on both sides, two alkenes can form; by [[zaitsev]] the major product is the alkene with more alkyl groups on the doubly bonded carbons (more substituted, more stable). Example: 2-bromopentane → pent-2-ene (81 %, major) + pent-1-ene (19 %).

blocks.name: zaitsev
blocks.title: Zaitsev's rule: which alkene is the major product?
blocks.caption: Choose a halide. See which alkene forms from each β-hydrogen and which one is the major product.

blocks.text: **Elimination versus substitution:** The two reactions compete. Small nucleophiles prefer substitution (SN2); bulky bases (e.g. tert-butoxide) cannot reach the carbon, so they pull off a β-hydrogen and cause elimination. Primary halides show SN2, tertiary halides SN1 or elimination; secondary halides depend on the concentration of the base.

**Reaction with metals:** An alkyl halide and Mg in dry ether give a **[[grignard]]** (R–MgX). The C–Mg bond is covalent but polar (R^{δ−}–Mg^{δ+}); so it is very reactive and reacts with water, alcohols, amines etc. to give a hydrocarbon (RMgX + H₂O → RH + Mg(OH)X); it must therefore be kept free of water. **Wurtz reaction:** An alkyl halide with Na in dry ether gives a hydrocarbon with twice the carbon atoms (2RX + 2Na → R–R + 2NaX).

**Reactions of haloarenes:** Aryl halides are much less reactive in nucleophilic substitution, because: (i) **resonance** — the electron pair on the halogen can conjugate with the π-electrons of the ring, so the C–Cl bond gets partial double bond character (C–X 169 pm, against 177 pm in haloalkanes); (ii) the sp² carbon is more electronegative, so the C–X bond is stronger; (iii) the phenyl cation is unstable, so SN1 is not possible; (iv) the electron density of the ring repels the nucleophile.

An electron-withdrawing group (–NO₂) in the ortho or para position increases reactivity: chlorobenzene gives phenol with NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm, but p-nitrochlorobenzene reacts at 443 K, 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene at 368 K, and 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene even with warm water. This is because NO₂ carries the negative charge of the carbanion formed on attack by the nucleophile through resonance and so stabilises it; an NO₂ group in the meta position cannot take part in the resonance, so it has no effect.

blocks.name: aryl-nitro
blocks.title: Effect of the –NO₂ group
blocks.caption: Choose the number and position of –NO₂ groups and see the temperature needed for substitution and the resonance of the negative charge.

blocks.text: **Electrophilic substitution:** Halogens deactivate the benzene ring through the inductive effect (−I), but the resonance effect (+R) raises the electron density at the ortho and para positions. So the halogens are deactivating yet ortho-para directing. Halogenation (FeCl₃/Cl₂), nitration (HNO₃/H₂SO₄), sulphonation and Friedel–Crafts reactions of chlorobenzene give para (major) and ortho (minor) products. **Wurtz–Fittig reaction:** aryl halide + alkyl halide + Na (dry ether) → alkylbenzene; **Fittig reaction:** 2ArX + 2Na → Ar–Ar (diphenyl).

blocks.label: Example 5
blocks.text:
Why is chlorine ortho-para directing although it is electron-withdrawing?
By the inductive effect chlorine withdraws electrons and destabilises the intermediate carbocation (so the reaction is slow), but by resonance it donates electrons and stabilises the carbocation formed by ortho and para attack. Reactivity is controlled by the inductive effect and the directing property by resonance.
Compounds of carbon with more than one halogen atom are polyhalogen compounds. Most of them are useful in agriculture and industry, but some harm the environment and health:

items: **Dichloromethane (CH₂Cl₂):** a paint remover and solvent used in making aerosols; inhaling much of it harms the nervous system and the eyes, and causes vomiting.

**Trichloromethane (chloroform, CHCl₃):** a solvent; formerly an anaesthetic. In light and air it is oxidised to the very poisonous phosgene (COCl₂) — so it is stored in dark bottles filled to the brim.
**Triiodomethane (iodoform, CHI₃):** formerly an antiseptic; it is the iodine liberated from it that kills germs.
**Tetrachloromethane (CCl₄):** used in fire extinguishers and in making freons; it damages the liver, kidneys and heart, and rises into the atmosphere where it depletes the ozone layer.
**[[freon]]:** e.g. CCl₂F₂; non-toxic, unreactive and easily liquefied — used in refrigerators. In the stratosphere they produce free radicals that destroy the ozone layer.

**DDT (p,p′-dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane):** the first chlorinated insecticide; it helped control the insects that spread malaria and typhoid. But it is chemically stable and soluble in fats, so it accumulates in the fatty tissue of animals — and it has been banned in many countries.

summary: [[haloalkane]]s and [[haloarene]]s are classified by the number of halogens and the hybridisation of carbon. The C–X bond is polar; boiling points follow RI > RBr > RCl > RF.
Preparation: from alcohols (SOCl₂ is best), from hydrocarbons, by halogen exchange (Finkelstein, Swarts) and from amines (Sandmeyer).
[[sn2]]: one step, second order, inversion, CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°. [[sn1]]: two steps, first order, carbocation, racemisation, 3° > 2° > 1°.
[[chiral]] molecules contain an asymmetric carbon; the two [[enantiomer]]s rotate light oppositely; a [[racemic]] mixture is optically inactive. SN2 → inversion, SN1 → racemisation.
In elimination [[zaitsev]]: the more substituted alkene is the major product. [[grignard]] RMgX is very reactive; the Wurtz reaction gives R–R.
Aryl halides are less reactive in substitution because of resonance; an ortho/para –NO₂ increases reactivity. In electrophilic substitution halogens are deactivating but ortho-para directing.
Polyhalogen compounds (CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CHI₃, CCl₄, [[freon]], DDT) are useful, but some do not decompose easily and harm the environment.
